overview.text: Subutai, also spelled Subedei, was a Mongol commander who served Genghis Khan and later his successors. He and Jebe led a western raid that defeated a coalition of Rus' princes and Cuman allies at the Kalka River in 1223. Under Genghis's successor Ögedei, Subutai helped direct the much larger campaign into the Rus' principalities and central Europe. Prince Batu held senior dynastic command, while Subutai provided experienced military leadership. In 1241 Mongol forces defeated King Béla IV of Hungary at Mohi, using coordinated movements around the Sajó River. Subutai's career links the empire's earlier raids with its later western conquests; he was a general, not a khan.

He was a leading commander in the western campaign under Prince Batu.
The Mongols defeated Hungary's King Béla IV at Mohi in 1241.
Subutai's troops used river crossings and flanking movements at Mohi.

overview.text: The Nigerian Civil War, fought from 1967 to January 1970, began after leaders in southeastern Nigeria declared an independent Republic of Biafra. Political crises, military coups, and ethnic violence after independence had shattered trust among regions. Nigeria's federal government fought to keep the country united, while Biafran forces tried to defend secession. Fighting occurred mainly in the southeast. Lost access to imported food and obstacles to relief deliveries left many civilians without adequate food; hunger and disease killed large numbers of people, especially children. Biafra's military defeat ended the secession, but the war left long memories and debates over the treatment of civilians and regional belonging.

overview.text: Auschwitz-Birkenau was a Nazi German concentration-camp and extermination complex near Oświęcim in German-occupied Poland. Auschwitz I opened in 1940, initially imprisoning Polish political prisoners among others. Auschwitz II-Birkenau began operating in 1942 and became the complex's principal site of mass murder, especially of Jews deported from across Europe. Prisoners also included Roma and Sinti, Soviet prisoners of war, and people of other nationalities. Some were forced into labor; many were killed on arrival or died through deliberate deprivation. The notorious 'Arbeit macht frei' inscription stood over the gate of Auschwitz I, not Birkenau. The preserved site is a memorial to the victims of Nazi persecution and genocide.

overview.text: F. W. de Klerk was South Africa's state president from 1989 to 1994, during the transition away from apartheid, the system of enforced racial segregation and white minority rule. In February 1990 he announced the legalization of the African National Congress and other banned organizations; Nelson Mandela was released days later after 27 years in prison. Negotiations between the government and liberation movements proceeded amid continuing political violence. Domestic resistance, international pressure, and economic strain had helped make apartheid unsustainable. De Klerk and Mandela shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize. After South Africa's first national election with voters of all races in 1994, Mandela became president and de Klerk served as a deputy president in the unity government.

overview.text: Quintus Fabius Maximus was a Roman commander and politician during the Second Punic War against Carthage. After Hannibal's victories in Italy, Rome appointed Fabius dictator in 217 BCE. He avoided a decisive battle with Hannibal's formidable army, instead following it, harassing detachments, and limiting its access to supplies. Critics saw his caution as weakness, but his approach helped Rome preserve forces while it fought a longer war. He earned the name Cunctator, meaning 'the Delayer,' and the term Fabian strategy later came to describe calculated delay. Fabius did not win the war alone: Roman success also depended on other commanders and campaigns, culminating in Hannibal's defeat in 202 BCE.

overview.text: The Young Turks were Ottoman reformers associated especially with the Committee of Union and Progress, or CUP. In the 1908 revolution they pressed for constitutional government after years of rule under Sultan Abdülhamid II. Their early language promised political equality and modernization, but the movement was not uniform and its leadership changed course. CUP leaders consolidated dictatorial power in 1913 and took the empire into the First World War. Under the CUP-controlled Ottoman government, Armenians were systematically deported and murdered in 1915–1916, in the Armenian genocide. The movement's history therefore includes both a challenge to autocracy and later state violence; responsibility for the genocide rests with the government and its agents.

The Committee of Union and Progress was a central Young Turk organization.
Early reformers advocated a constitutional regime.
CUP leaders seized dictatorial power in 1913.

overview.text: Leon Trotsky was a revolutionary who joined the Bolsheviks in 1917 and became a major leader in the new Soviet state. As war commissar, he organized the Red Army during the Russian Civil War, relying on discipline and military expertise to fight the Bolsheviks' opponents. He argued for international revolution and later clashed with Joseph Stalin over the Soviet Union's direction and control of the Communist movement. Expelled from party leadership and driven into exile, Trotsky helped establish the Fourth International in 1938 as an alternative to the Stalin-dominated Communist International. A Soviet agent attacked him in Mexico in 1940; he died from the wound. His career spans revolutionary power, civil war, and opposition in exile.

overview.text: The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, or UNCLOS, is a 1982 treaty setting a broad legal framework for ocean use. It entered into force in 1994. It defines maritime zones, including a territorial sea of up to 12 nautical miles and an exclusive economic zone, or EEZ, extending no more than 200 nautical miles from coastal baselines. Within an EEZ, a coastal state has rights to explore and manage resources such as fish and seabed minerals, while other states retain navigation and overflight freedoms. The convention also addresses marine environmental protection, scientific research, the deep seabed, and dispute settlement. An EEZ gives specific resource rights, not complete sovereignty over all activities at sea.

overview.text: Catherine of Aragon was a Spanish princess and Henry VIII's first wife, serving as queen consort of England from their marriage in 1509 until its annulment in 1533. She had earlier married Henry's elder brother Arthur, who died soon afterward. Catherine and Henry had several children, but only Mary, later Queen Mary I, survived childhood. Catherine also acted as regent while Henry campaigned in France in 1513, when England faced a Scottish invasion. Henry later sought to annul their marriage, arguing that her earlier marriage made it invalid; Catherine insisted the marriage was lawful. The pope refused Henry's request, but an English church court declared the marriage null in 1533, amid Henry's break with Rome.

overview.text: The Axis Powers were the wartime alliance centered on Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy, and imperial Japan during the Second World War. The three formalized their partnership in the Tripartite Pact of September 1940, and several other European states later joined. Each pursued expansion in its own region; the alliance promised mutual support but never operated through one unified military command. Axis invasions and occupations brought widespread destruction, including the Holocaust and other mass persecution. In April 1941 Axis forces invaded and partitioned Yugoslavia after a coup overturned its short-lived agreement with the pact. Italy surrendered to the Allies in 1943; Germany and Japan were defeated in 1945. The Axis opposed the Allied coalition.

The Axis never had a single unified military command.
